idiom_name: modules as mixins (include) plus Forwardable/DelegateClass for the crossing calls
implementation_notes: A Ruby class has one superclass but can include any number of modules, and the instance methods of a module run with the including object as self, so they read and write that object's instance variables ('instance methods appear as methods in a class when the module is included' - Module docs): one object carries both hierarchies' behaviour without a second object. For the crossing half, Forwardable generates the delegation the twin link would need - def_delegator :@target, :method, :alias and def_delegators - and DelegateClass delegates a whole class; the library documentation offers Forwardable explicitly 'as an alternative to inheritance'. The classic two-object pair is still justified when two independently registered objects are genuinely required (an object in a widget/observer list plus an object in a scheduler list) or when the second provider is not a module you can include.
code_sketch:
module Suspendable                      # mixin: behaviour, no second object
  def toggle_suspended
    @suspended = !@suspended
  end
end
class BallItem < GameItem               # one object, one superclass
  include Suspendable                   # the second hierarchy's code
  extend Forwardable
  def_delegator :@driver, :apply_suspended   # generated forwarding to the twin
  def initialize(driver) = (@driver = driver)
end
pitfalls: Cooperative initialisation matters: Module#include inserts the module after the class, so a module that defines initialize must call super or the second mixin never initialises.

Forwardable defines methods with define_method at class-definition time - the docs note that RDoc does not see them - and nothing fails at load time if the target method is missing; the NoMethodError appears at call time.
method_missing/delegate-based forwarding needs respond_to_missing? as well, or respond_to? and tools that rely on it (serializers, testing frameworks) report wrong answers.

Instance variables are per object, so a module mixed into two classes shares code but never state; if both aspects need their own value, name the variables per aspect instead of hoping one variable serves both.
